title: 一款本地 LLM 面对 15 道新论文问题全答错，尽管原文段落就在眼前
author: Waleed Esmail

Local LLMs Handle Textbook RAG but Fail on New Research Papers

Five setups, one blind grading pack: textbook scores ran 12 to 20 of 20, but a paper published this year dropped them to 0 to 9 of 15.

Waleed Esmail
November 16, 20269 min read
Prefer us on Google

I read a lot of technical material: machine learning textbooks, particle physics, and papers in my own field. I wanted an assistant that answers questions about my library, cites the exact page, shows me the passage, and runs on my own laptop. No uploads, no subscription, no guessing where an answer came from.

So I built one!

To be honest about how: I didn't type most of the code myself. Claude Code built it on my machine, phase by phase, while I designed it, wrote the test questions, read every report and decided at every gate. That way of working is a story on its own. This post is about what the measurements showed, because some of it surprised me.

The short version: on textbook questions, small local models do well. On a paper published this year, they collapse to almost zero, with the same retrieval, the same prompt and the same passages in front of them. If you build a local RAG system, how new your material is to the model matters more than how hard the question sounds.

Learn this step by step with the interactive AI Engineer roadmap.

What I built, in one picture

The app is a FastAPI server with a React front end. You drop PDFs and PowerPoint decks into a folder. Each document is parsed once with Docling, display equations are read again by Granite-Docling and checked against the PDF's own glyphs, and the text is cut into 300–600-token chunks that never split an equation, a table or a code block.

A question goes through keyword search (BM25) and vector search (bge-m3), the two ranked lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion, and a cross-encoder reranks the top 30 down to 6. The top hits bring their neighbouring chunks, and a few reserved slots add figures, summaries and my own notes. Then the model I chose writes an answer with numbered citations, and any citation to a source it was never given is removed before I see it.

There are four answer modes:

  • Fast: gpt-oss-20b on my GPU. Free, about 17 s.

  • Balanced: Gemma 4 26B-A4B on my GPU. Free, about a minute, can look at images.

  • Qwen: Qwen3.8-27B through OpenRouter, pinned to one provider. About $0.015 a question.

  • Deep: Claude Opus 5.5. About $0.14 a question.

Local is the default. Hosted is a per-question choice, and the app says exactly what it sends.

How I measured

Before writing the retrieval code, I wrote 35 gold questions from my own sources: 20 from four textbooks and 15 from a paper of mine published this year. For each I wrote down the expected pages and the key points a good answer must contain. For the 20 textbook questions I also listed the facts that must reach the model.

Every answer was graded good, weak, or wrong by fresh grader agents that hadn't seen the work. Answers from several runs were shuffled into one anonymised pack, without model names, and each answer was shown with the passages it was given. That last detail turned out to be the most useful one: it lets you tell a model that reasoned badly from a model that never saw the fact.

Finding 1: the textbook/paper split

To separate "small model" from "local runtime", I ran the same 35 questions through five setups: three open models via an API at full precision, the same gpt-oss locally, and Opus as the reference. All with the same retrieval and the same prompt, graded in one blind pack.

On the textbooks, the scores were 20, 19, 16, 12 and 12 out of 20. Fine. On the paper they were 9, 7, 1, 2 and 0 out of 15.

Read that again: the passages were in front of every model. The local gpt-oss got the same passages as Opus and still got zero of the paper questions right.

My reading: on textbook material the small models have seen the ideas many times. The passages only need to remind them. On a new paper, the answer has to be built from the passages alone, and that is where small models fall apart. They fill gaps with what usually comes next in a textbook, not with what the paper says.

Two side results made this cleaner:

  • Quantisation is not the problem. gpt-oss through an API at native precision scored like my local copy (14 vs 12 good, sign test p = 0.69). The local QAT Gemma matched its full-precision API twin too. On this hardware the limit is the model, not the runtime.

  • A mid-size hosted model is close to the frontier. Qwen3.8-27B was not significantly behind Opus (26 vs 29), for about a tenth of the price per question. It is slow, though: about three minutes per answer, almost all of it thinking.

So the mode advice in my app is simple: Fast for looking things up in books you know, Deep or Qwen for anything new.

Finding 2: most failures were retrieval failures

Grading answers together with their passages showed something else. Again and again, a bad answer happened because the fact never reached the model, not because the model reasoned badly.

  • Figures. I wrote 10 questions whose answers live only in a plot. Deep got 1 of 10. Nine failures were retrieval: no passage contained the value. I had every figure described once (397 figures, $3.50 with Sonnet 5.5) so search can find them, and the image itself goes to the model when its figure is retrieved. Result: 9 of 10.

  • Overview questions. "What is chapter 12 about and how does it build on chapter 9?" No single chunk holds a chapter's argument. A local model wrote a summary tree (sections, chapters, whole document: 281 summaries in 2.9 hours, $0). Overview questions went from 1 of 8 to 8 of 8. On the full 16-question set, 16 good against 8, with no question good only without the tree (p = 0.008).

  • Neighbour chunks. A chunk boundary often falls between the sentence that matches and the equation you need. Adding two neighbours each way around the top three hits took the share of book questions with every needed fact retrieved from 16/20 to 19/20.

None of these changed the model. All of them changed what the model could see.

Finding 3: where local models broke, even with good inputs

Some jobs I tried hard to keep local and couldn't:

  • Reading figures. I compared four describers blind on ten figures. Gemma 4 (thinking on or off) and Qwen3-VL 8B misread axis scales, one by a factor of about 25, and invented values. Qwen3-VL invented seven values across the ten figures. Sonnet 5.5 got 9 good of 10 in my own blind rating.

  • Reading web pages. With web search, Deep went from 3–4 to 11 of 11 good on questions the library couldn't answer. Balanced got 2 of 11. Even when the app chose the pages itself and handed Balanced clean excerpts, it was still 2 of 11. It misread the pages: a 5.8σ tension became 8– σ\sigma , a Python version was off by one.

  • Writing checkable claims. I added a checker: the model writes its derivation's claims in a small block, and SymPy checks each one, units included. Deep wrote checkable claims in 10 of 10 derivations. The local models did in 2 to 6 of 10, and their errors were mostly outside the claims they wrote. Best-of-N resampling on failed checks gave no gain (4 good with or without it).

And one I didn't expect: offering a tool can hurt. Balanced scored 21 good without a "propose a web search" tool and 17 with it, on the same library questions, none of which needed a web search. For small models, every extra tool is another decision they can get wrong.

Finding 4: with 35 questions, know your noise

This part saved me from fooling myself more than once.

  • Graders drift. The same set of answers graded in two different rounds moved by up to 3 good answers. So I only compare runs inside one blind pack.

  • Use the sign test. For two runs on the same questions, only the questions where they disagree carry information. The summary tree won 8–0: p = 2.2−82.2^{-8} ≈ 0.008. Real. In my final evaluation, Balanced lost 4 answers and gained 1 against its reference: p = 0.375. Noise.

  • Use intervals. Deep's 29 of 35 in an early round sounds like "83%". The Wilson 95% interval is 67% to 92%.

  • Estimate the swing. If each of 32 answers is good with probability about 0.55, the difference between two runs has a standard deviation of (2⋅32⋅0.55⋅0.45) \sqrt{(2·32·0.55·0.45)} ≈ 4 answers. A drop of 3 is less than one standard deviation.

None of this is advanced statistics. It takes ten minutes to learn, and it changes which results you believe.

What I'd tell you before you build one

  1. Write the test questions first, from your own material, with key points. A test set written after the system tends to test what you built.

  2. Grade with the passages visible. It tells you whether to fix retrieval or change the model.

  3. Split your questions by novelty. Report "familiar" and "new" material separately. A single average hides the most important difference.

  4. Fix retrieval before you buy a bigger model. Neighbours, a reranker, figure descriptions and a summary tree gave me more than any model swap.

  5. Let small models do small jobs. Keep their tool list short. Route figures, web pages and derivations to a stronger model, and say so in the interface.

  6. Fix the bar before the run, and report misses as misses. Several of my gates failed; each was decided openly.

  7. Show the source. Every answer cites its page, and a click opens it. When the model is wrong, I see it in seconds.

Closing

The final version answers 34 of my 35 gold questions well in Deep, for about 14 cents a question. Fast answers textbook lookups for free in about 17 seconds. The two together cover most of my daily use, and I always know where an answer came from.

The most useful thing I learned is not in the code. A local model is a good librarian for material that looks like what it was trained on, and an unreliable reader of anything new. Build for that, and measure it.

Thank you for reading. The code is open source under AGPL-3.0: https://github.com/wesmail/study-assistant-share. Try it on your own library, open an issue when something breaks, and send me the questions it gets wrong. That’s how the measurements get better.

summary: 本文介绍了一项实证研究：研究者使用 35 道标准答案题目，对比了 5 种不同的模型配置（三种基于 API 的开放模型、本地 gpt-oss-20b，以及 Claude Opus 5.5），其中 20 道题来自教科书，15 道来自一篇新发表的研究论文。研究采用相同的检索方式和提示词，结果发现，各模型在教科书题目上的得分为 12-20/20，而在新论文题目上的得分则降至 0-9/15。本地 gpt-oss-20b 在教科书题目上得分为 12/20，但面对新论文时即使拿到了相同的段落，仍得了 0/15。作者据此总结，小型本地模型处理熟悉的教科书内容表现不错，但难以应对新研究论文，并建议已知书籍使用 Fast 模式，新材料则使用 Deep/Qwen。其他发现包括：量化并非性能瓶颈；改进检索（补充图表描述、摘要树和相邻文本块）带来的提升大于升级模型；小模型在读取图表和理解网页内容方面表现不佳。

mainPoints.point: 本地模型擅长处理教科书 RAG，却难以应对新研究论文
mainPoints.explanation: 小模型在教科书题目上得分为 12-20/20，但在一篇新发表的论文上降至 0-9/15，尽管两者使用了相同的段落和检索方式。这表明，模型对训练数据的熟悉程度才是关键因素，而非问题难度。

mainPoints.point: 改进检索带来的提升大于升级模型
mainPoints.explanation: 加入图表描述、摘要树和相邻文本块，比换用更大的模型更能提升表现。图表题的正确数从 1/10 提升到 9/10，概览题从 1/8 提升到 8/8，而在检索到所有事实的情况下，书籍相关题目的正确数从 16/20 提升到 19/20。

mainPoints.point: 量化并非本地模型的性能瓶颈
mainPoints.explanation: 本地 gpt-oss-20b 与其 API 版本的表现相近（分别有 14 道和 12 道题答对），这表明性能上限取决于模型架构和规模，而非量化。

mainPoints.point: 小模型难以胜任图表读取、网页解读等专业任务
mainPoints.explanation: Gemma 4 和 Qwen3-VL 误读了坐标轴刻度，并在图表描述中编造数值；而网页搜索将 Deep 的正确答案数从 3-4/11 提升至 11/11，表明有些任务需要能力更强的模型。

keyQuotes: 相同的问题、相同的检索：针对 20 道教科书题和 15 道新论文题，给出好答案，并进行一轮盲评。
在教科书题目上，得分分别为 20、19、16、12 和 12，满分均为 20。还不错。在论文题目上，得分分别为 9、7、1、2 和 0，满分均为 15。
本地 gpt-oss 拿到了和 Opus 相同的段落，但论文题目一道都没答对。
对于看起来像训练材料的内容，本地模型是个好图书管理员；但面对任何新内容，它都是个不可靠的读者。
先改进检索，再买更大的模型。相邻文本块、重排序器、图表描述和摘要树带来的提升，比我换任何模型都大。
